trial_name: ProMISe — Trial of Early, Goal-Directed Resuscitation for Septic Shock (2015)
citation: Mouncey PR, Osborn TM, Power GS, et al. Trial of early, goal-directed resuscitation for septic shock. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(14):1301-1311.
trial_type: Pragmatic, multicenter, open-label, 1:1 randomized controlled trial
one_liner: In UK emergency departments, a 6-hour protocolised early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) resuscitation bundle did not decrease 90-day mortality compared to clinician-led usual care.

pico.population: Adults presenting to the ED with early septic shock or severe sepsis with hyperlactatemia (SIRS >= 2 plus refractory hypotension or blood lactate >= 4 mmol/L).
pico.intervention: Protocolised 6-hour EGDT resuscitation bundle targeting CVP >= 8 mmHg, MAP >= 65 mmHg, and ScvO2 >= 70% with mandated central line placement and triggered blood transfusions/dobutamine.
pico.comparison: Usual resuscitation without mandated CVP/ScvO2 targets, transfusion algorithms, or dobutamine protocols.

background.existing_knowledge: The single-center Rivers et al. (2001) trial reported a substantial mortality reduction in septic shock using a 6-hour early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) protocol targeting CVP, MAP, and ScvO2.
background.knowledge_gap: By 2015, standard ED sepsis care routinely incorporated early antibiotics, lactate testing, and aggressive fluid/vasopressor resuscitation, creating uncertainty about whether mandated invasive EGDT provided incremental benefit.
background.hypothesis: A protocolised 6-hour EGDT resuscitation strategy reduces 90-day all-cause mortality compared with clinician-led usual resuscitation in ED patients with early septic shock.

methods.design: Pragmatic, open-label, parallel-group 1:1 RCT across 56 UK National Health Service (NHS) hospitals with a published prespecified statistical analysis plan.
methods.setting: 56 UK NHS emergency departments with planned critical care admission capacity and no existing routine EGDT protocols; enrolment occurred between 2011 and 2014.

inclusion: Refractory hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg after >= 1,000 mL fluid within 60 min) OR hyperlactatemia (blood lactate >= 4 mmol/L)
exclusion: Already admitted to critical care during current admission
Comfort measures only / treatment limitation decisions
Contraindication to central venous catheterization or protocol components

methods.intervention: Protocolised 6-hour EGDT bundle delivered by trained clinical staff. Targeted hierarchical goals: CVP >= 8 mmHg (IV fluids), MAP >= 65 mmHg or SBP >= 90 mmHg (vasopressors/vasodilators), and ScvO2 >= 70% (packed red blood cell transfusion to hematocrit/hemoglobin targets and/or dobutamine infusion). Mandatory CVC placement.
methods.comparison: Usual resuscitation at clinician discretion without mandated CVP/ScvO2 targets, central venous line placement, transfusion triggers, or dobutamine algorithms.
methods.blinding: Open-label intervention (blinding not feasible); primary mortality outcome assessed objectively via national registry tracking.
methods.sample_size_power: 1,260 patients (630 per arm) to detect an 8% absolute mortality reduction (40% to 32%) with 90% power at a two-sided 5% significance level.
secondary_outcomes: In-hospital mortality (death before acute hospital discharge)
Receipt of advanced cardiovascular support during index admission
SOFA score at 6 hours and 72 hours
Total costs per patient to 90 days
methods.follow_up: 90 days for primary endpoint, quality of life, and healthcare resource utilization.

headline_bullets: 90-day mortality was virtually identical between EGDT and usual care (29.5% vs 29.2%, RR 1.01, P=0.90).
EGDT markedly increased procedural and pharmacological intensity, including dobutamine (18.1% vs 2.4%) and blood transfusions (8.8% vs 3.7%).
Organ dysfunction trajectories (SOFA scores at 6h and 72h) were equivalent between groups.
EGDT increased mean 90-day costs by £989 per patient without producing any QALY gain.

outcomes_table.note: Increased cardiovascular support in EGDT arm
No difference in early organ dysfunction
No separation in later organ dysfunction

outcomes_table.outcome: Total costs to 90 days (£ mean ± SD)
outcomes_table.note: Higher mean costs per patient in EGDT group
Modest increase in early fluid volume

safety: Serious adverse events occurred in 30/625 (4.8%) in EGDT vs 26/623 (4.2%) in usual care (RR 1.16; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.93; P=0.58).
EGDT significantly increased procedural invasive risks (CVC insertion 92.1% vs 50.9%) and pharmacological risks (dobutamine 18.1% vs 2.4%; transfusion 8.8% vs 3.7%).

domains.notes: Central randomisation with site stratification; allocation concealed until enrolment.
Open-label design carries potential risk for non-protocolised decisions, but primary outcome (mortality) is objective.
Minimal loss post-randomisation (6/630 in EGDT, 11/630 in usual care withdrawn/excluded); primary ITT analysis intact.
Clear process separation; usual care included high background invasive line placement (50.9% CVC, 59.6% arterial lines).
Well balanced: mean age 66.4 vs 64.3; APACHE II 18.7 vs 18.0; median pre-randomisation fluids 2,000 mL in both groups.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is strong with robust outcome objectivity and minimal missing data.

domains.notes: Adult ED patients with early septic shock across 56 NHS hospitals; 90-day mortality (~29%) reflects contemporary high-income care.
Highly applicable to healthcare systems with mature sepsis pathways and rapid baseline antimicrobial/fluid delivery.

external_validity.verdict: High generalisability to emergency and critical care settings in modern high-income health systems.

strengths: Large pragmatic multicenter trial across 56 UK hospitals
Early randomisation (median 2.5 hours from ED arrival)
Clear process-of-care separation achieved between arms
Objective primary endpoint with prespecified analysis plan
Integrated health economics and quality-of-life evaluation
limitations: Open-label design unable to blind clinicians to intervention
Substantial baseline invasive monitoring in usual care (50.9% CVC use)
Lower baseline mortality than anticipated (29% actual vs 40% projected), reducing power for small effect sizes
Evaluated a rigid protocol combining static pressure and venous saturation triggers

critical_appraisal.summary: A definitive pragmatic trial establishing that mandatory ScvO2-targeted EGDT provides no benefit over clinician-guided resuscitation when standard sepsis care is delivered promptly.
strengths: Rigorous design and execution across a national network
Complete 90-day follow-up with robust economic data
weaknesses: High baseline quality of usual care limiting contrast

sections.authors_conclusion: In patients presenting to the emergency department with early septic shock, protocolised early goal-directed therapy did not reduce 90-day all-cause mortality compared with usual resuscitation, while increasing resource use.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: De-adopt routine ScvO2/CVP-driven protocolised EGDT; focus resuscitation on rapid sepsis identification, early antibiotics, IV fluids, and vasopressors.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult patients presenting to the emergency department with septic shock or severe sepsis with hyperlactatemia.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean early resuscitation is ineffective; it shows that rigid protocolised invasive targets add no benefit over timely standard care.
implementation_caveats: Usual care in ProMISe delivered median 2,000 mL fluids prior to randomisation and rapid antimicrobial therapy.
Dynamic markers of organ perfusion should guide escalation rather than routine CVP/ScvO2 catheters.

controversies.notes: Since Rivers (2001), usual care evolved to integrate early fluids and antibiotics, eliminating the incremental benefit of mandated EGDT protocols.
EGDT increased CVC placements, dobutamine infusions, and transfusions, increasing mean costs by £989 per patient without clinical gain.
Highlighted the clinical inadequacy of static CVP and ScvO2 measurements as targets for tissue perfusion.

context_related_trials.relation: Original single-center RCT that established 6-hour EGDT bundle showing significant survival benefit, which ProMISe re-evaluated.
US multicenter trial showing no mortality benefit with EGDT vs protocolised standard or usual care.
Australasian multicenter trial demonstrating equal 90-day survival between EGDT and usual resuscitation.
Individual patient data meta-analysis of ProCESS, ARISE, and ProMISe confirming no benefit of EGDT across all subgroups.

unresolved_questions: Role of advanced hemodynamic monitoring in select refractory septic shock non-responders.
Optimal fluid titration algorithms based on dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Mandated ScvO2/CVP-targeted EGDT increases invasive procedures and costs without improving survival in modern septic shock resuscitation.
